subject: Business
title: Fiat Currency: Money by Government Decree
description: A 60-second lesson on Fiat Currency: Money by Government Decree.

hook.text: A dollar bill costs 12 cents to print. Its face value is $1. The difference is pure government authority.

buildup.text: Fiat money has value because the government declares it legal tender — not because it's backed by gold or silver.

discovery.text: Every major currency today is fiat. The US dollar, euro, yen, and pound are all backed by institutional trust.

twist.text: Fiat gives governments flexibility to manage economies. It also gives them the power to debase currencies.

climax.text: No fiat currency has survived forever. The average lifespan of a fiat currency is 27 years.

punchline.text: Your money is worth something because everyone agrees it is. For now.

quiz.question: What gives fiat currency its value?
options: The gold stored in central bank vaults
The paper and ink it's printed on

details.summary: Fiat currency has value because a government declares it legal tender, not because it is backed by a physical commodity like gold. Every major currency today is fiat, deriving its value from public trust in the issuing government and its economic management.
details.whyItMatters: Fiat money enables flexible monetary policy that commodity-backed systems cannot provide, but it also introduces the risk of inflation when governments create too much money. Understanding fiat explains both its power and its vulnerabilities.
takeaways: Fiat money derives value from government decree rather than commodity backing
Every major world currency today operates as fiat money
The risk is that governments can print unlimited amounts, causing inflation

faq.question: What prevents fiat money from becoming worthless?
faq.answer: Government demand for tax payments in the official currency creates baseline demand. Central bank credibility in managing inflation maintains trust. The legal requirement to accept it for debts, combined with a functioning economy, sustains its value as a medium of exchange.

faq.question: Has fiat currency ever completely failed?
faq.answer: Yes. Zimbabwe's dollar, Venezuela's bolivar, and Weimar Germany's mark all collapsed through hyperinflation when governments printed excessive money. However, most fiat currencies managed by independent central banks with inflation targets maintain stable value for decades.
